newsitem.title: USA: Japan rates called factor behind high-yield bubble.
newsitem.headline: Japan rates called factor behind high-yield bubble.

text.p: The low cost of raising capital in Japan is one likely factor behind the global rush into high-yielding financial instruments such as U.S. junk bonds and high-risk emerging market debt, according to experts.

The dramatic narrowing of spreads between high-risk and benchmark rates led Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan to warn in his Congressional testimony on Wednesday about the "perception of low risk, possibly unrealistically low risk" priced into junk bond issues.
"This optimistic attitude has become especially evident in quality spreads on high-yield corporate bonds, what we used to call 'junk bonds,'" Greenspan said.

Goldman, Sachs International vice chairman Robert Hormats said the narrowing of the spreads was likely a function of cheap funding in Japan that allows daring investors to compete for high-yield instruments since the cost of such play is not punishing.
"It's a great trade, a great arbitrage. You get cheap money in a weakening currency, and you buy high-yielding assets in a strengthening currency," Hormats said.

The Bank of Japan (BoJ) has kept its benchmark discount rate at 0.50 percent since September 1995 and money market rates in Japan are at one-third of 1.0 percent. Since that date, the dollar has appreciated by about 25 percent versus the yen.

The coincidental depreciation of the yen and the rally in a huge variety of financial instruments -- including those regarded as very high risks such as the Russian debt -- indicates that part of the funding originates from Japan.
"As long as it lasts, it's a great deal. It may indeed last because the odds of the Bank of Japan raising rates and the Fed lowering rates are almost zero," Hormats predicted.
The Goldman vice chairman acknowledged it is not possible to track down international flows generated in Japan and parked in other markets, such as the U.S. junk bond market.

The U.S. Treasury publishes data about international capital flows into U.S. markets with a three-month lag. While the data show where flows are orginiating, it does not indicate where the foreign investor raised capital.
"People get cheap money in Japan and buy high-yielding assets elsewhere. We don't know the magnitude of that trade, but it is obviously substantial," Hormats added.
Hormats agreed with other experts that the overcrowding of the main U.S. markets, such as stocks, has led other, more speculative investors to chase higher returns.

"We have seen huge flows of money into the U.S. and other markets, and perhaps, Japan is the ultimate source (for this)," said Merrill Lynch chief high-yield strategist Martin Fridson who noted high-yield corporate spreads narrowed by about 100 basis points in 1996.
Fridson added that high-yield spreads reflect credit risk, liquidity, and monetary conditions and that they are currently priced accordingly -- mainly given the liquidity.

"Right now, it (spread) is pretty much in line (with such parameters), given that the default rate is fairly low, given the very strong inflows of capital into the secondary market, and the extraordinarily favorable monetary environment," Fridson said.
"The real question is what will happen going forward. If those conditions change, the spread will certainly widen. The question is when," Fridson stressed.
Fridson agreed with Hormats there are no data readily available to prove that the source of funds fueling the rally came from Japan.
But he pointed out that U.S. high-yield spreads, after their sharp narrowing in 1996, tightened again by an additional 25 percent in January 1997 alone.

This coincided with the 1996 dollar/yen rally and a sharp appreciation in January, an indication funds were raised in Japan and converted into the currency of the foreign country where they were parked.
But Fridson said another theory regarding the high-yields rally is that "we are in the new era of structural changes, that history should be thrown out."

Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler said rallies in a variety of instruments are being fueled by international capital flows reflecting the increased globalization of markets.

"The money is coming from a variety of sources, mutual funds, institutional funds, from all over the world, and it is difficult to pinpoint where the junk bond market is drawing its funds from," Resler said.

"But it's a noted phenomenon investors chase yields when they find yields on conventional debt relatively low," added Resler who agreed "where else but in Japan are interest rates so low if you look at the cost of funding?"
Still, Resler cautioned the low cost of funding can only offset to a certain extent the risks linked to high-yielding investments.
"Whether or not investors are snatching high-yield securities at an inadequate risk premium compared to their underlying value is the real issue the market will face," he concluded.
